Thanksgiving can leave loaded trailers sitting for days while terminals close and fewer employees are around to watch them. Before the break, carriers should figure out where freight will be parked and how it will be protected.
What’s Related
J. J. Keller ’s Josh Lovan, a former undercover detective and carrier safety director, is urging carriers to secure freight before the holiday. His white paper, Cargo Security and Preventing Theft in Trucking , outlines steps they can take.
1. Plan where freight will sit
Start with parking. Keller recommends well-lit spots with controlled access, fencing, and cameras, and says to avoid leaving loaded trailers unattended whenever possible.
The white paper calls for locking loaded inbound and outbound trailers during closed hours. It also lists four ways to secure loaded trailers during closures or whenever they are unattended: padlocked, docked, butted or blocked.
For security-sensitive freight, back swing-door trailers against a dock and overhead-door trailers against another trailer. Keller recommends both padlocks and kingpin locks for these loads.
Door locks restrict access to cargo , while kingpin locks help prevent unauthorized hookup to a tractor. Straight trucks and pickup-and- delivery trailers should have their cargo compartments locked away from the terminal except during loading and unloading.
RELATED STORIES: Fake Pickups Top the Worry List as Cargo Theft Gets More Organized | Half of Cargo Theft Cases Now Linked to Trusted Carriers
2. Check the yard and keep watch
Before closing, check gates, lighting, cameras, and alarms. The paper lists high-definition cameras that retain at least 60 days of footage among its suggested security measures.
Drivers leaving a truck unattended at a closed terminal should shut off the engine, close the windows, and lock the doors. The key should go with the manifest in the terminal’s designated spot.
GPS tracking and tamper alerts can flag unexpected movement or interference with a shipment . Carriers should also set driver and dispatcher check-in procedures and make clear how to report suspicious activity.
3. Inspect loads and document problems
Drivers should verify loads before leaving and check seals at every stop. The paper recommends documenting high-value goods with photos, serial numbers, and other identifying details that could help establish what went missing.
Only the designated supervisor should have access to the seal supply, and a distribution log should be maintained. Before accepting trailers from a railroad yard or another carrier, drivers should check seal integrity, record the seal number, and report discrepancies immediately.
“There is no single lock, camera or piece of technology that will prevent every cargo theft,” Lovan said.
